title: Praying for healing
hook: Pentecostals pray boldly for healing, trusting God with the outcome

segments.voice: Yesterday, prophecy and discernment: a word spoken, then weighed. Your line was build up. Did your kind word find its person? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

"Is any sick among you?" That question sits in the letter of James, and the instructions that follow are practical. Call the elders of the church. Let them pray over the sick person, anointing with oil in the name of the Lord. In a Pentecostal service, that can look very direct. Near the end, the pastor invites anyone who is ill to come forward. Elders gather. Someone brings a small bottle of oil. Hands rest on shoulders, and the prayers are bold: out loud, by name, asking God to heal this body, this week. Then everyone goes home and lives with whatever happens next. Both of those belong to today: praying for healing.

James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up." Pentecostal churches take that at its word. If the letter says ask, then ask, and say it out loud. Today's line echoes Isaiah, the song of a servant who suffers for others: "he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Stripes here aren't lines on a flag. They're the welts a beating leaves on skin. The New Testament reads this song through Jesus, beaten and crucified, and picks it up in two places, in two directions. Matthew, after Jesus heals a crowd of sick people one evening, quotes the verse just before: "Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses." Peter's first letter quotes the stripes line itself, right after saying Christ bore our sins, so "that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness." So Christians read it in more than one way. Some Pentecostals hold that healing for the body is part of what Christ won on the cross, and pray with that confidence. Other Christians read the stripes first as healing from sin, and see bodily healing as a gift God gives as he wills. Catholic and Orthodox Christians draw on James's verses for a sacrament of anointing the sick. And then there's Paul. He had what he called a thorn in the flesh, and he writes, "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." The answer he records: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Bold asking, and open hands about the answer. Pentecostal prayer for healing tries to hold both.

Here's the practice: hold someone who is sick. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind who is ill right now. Say their name quietly. See where they are this minute: a hospital bed, a couch, a waiting room. If you pray, you can ask God plainly for their healing, by name, the way James's elders did, and then leave the outcome in God's hands. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with care, and notice one thing they might need from you this week. The bell holds the time.
Praying for healing. Asking God boldly to heal, as James describes, while trusting God with what comes.

Your line: by his stripes. Today, do the one thing you noticed for the person who is sick: a call, a meal, a ride, a message that says you're thinking of them. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: In Pentecostal churches, the sick are often invited forward during or after a service, and elders or the congregation lay hands on them, sometimes anoint them with oil, and pray aloud for healing; Catholic and Orthodox Christians also practice a sacrament of anointing the sick.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you have a thorn in the flesh, and you've asked the Lord three times to take it away. what answer does your letter record?
options: my grace is sufficient for thee.
fork.reveal: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Paul asked boldly, and wrote down an answer he hadn't asked for.

original.note: Hebrew, in Isaiah 53:5: a welt or bruise, the mark a blow leaves. The King James renders it stripes.

trapdoor: what you thought: stripes means lines, like on a flag.
what it means: the welts a beating leaves. Isaiah's suffering servant is wounded, and others are healed.
what a scholar hears: Matthew sets the chapter beside healing bodies; Peter sets the stripes line beside dying to sins. readers weigh both.

notes: Description of a Pentecostal healing service (invitation forward, elders, oil, hands, prayer aloud) is general; confirm. 'Pentecostals take that plainly' is a characterization; soften if needed.
Two readings given without ranking: healing in the atonement (held by some Pentecostals) and stripes read first as healing from sin with bodily healing as God wills. Confirm both are fairly put.
Catholic and Orthodox sacrament of anointing the sick (Unction) linked to James 5:14–15; confirm phrasing.
Original: חַבּוּרָה in Isaiah 53:5 (ubachavurato, 'and by his stripe/bruise'); confirm spelling, pointing and transliteration khah-boo-RAH.
Matthew 8:16 says Jesus healed 'all that were sick' that evening; the script says 'a crowd of sick people'. Matthew 8:17 quotes Isaiah 53:4, described as 'the verse just before'.
The fork's 'three times' comes from 'thrice' in 2 Corinthians 12:8.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): the King James text of Isaiah 53:5 reads 'with his stripes', not 'by his stripes' (the index carry is closer to 1 Peter 2:24, 'by whose stripes'); 'today's line comes from Isaiah' changed to 'echoes Isaiah'. All quotations checked against the KJV; no other change.

Editor pass: 'a whip' changed to 'a beating' (Isaiah 53:5 names no whip); 'Christians hear this song as being about Jesus' narrowed to what the New Testament itself does; 'Pentecostals take that plainly' recast as 'Pentecostal churches take that at its word'.
